deep.reconstruction:
Context: on the previous pages Gauss showed that y = 1 + (1/4)x^2 + (1/4)(9/16)x^4 + ... = sum_n [(2n-1)!!/(2n)!!]^2 x^(2n) satisfies 1/y = M(1+x,1-x). He also derived the hypergeometric ODE (x^3-x)y'' + (3x^2-1)y' + xy = 0. This page converts that series into a definite integral and draws a general theorem from it.

(1) Wallis-type integrals. ∫_0^π cos^2φ dφ = π/2, ∫_0^π cos^4φ dφ = (1/2)(3/4)π, ∫_0^π cos^6φ dφ = (1/2)(3/4)(5/6)π, and ∫_0^π dφ = π. In general ∫_0^π cos^(2n)φ dφ = π (2n-1)!!/(2n)!!.

(2) Integral form of y. The binomial series is (1-u)^(-1/2) = Σ [(2n-1)!!/(2n)!!] u^n. Put u = x^2 cos^2φ and integrate term by term over [0,π] (this step is implicit, mine). Each x^(2n) coefficient picks up a second factor (2n-1)!!/(2n)!!. Hence ∫_0^π dφ/√(1-x^2cos^2φ) = π·Σ[(2n-1)!!/(2n)!!]^2 x^(2n) = π y, with x held constant. In modern terms ∫_0^π dφ/√(1-x^2cos^2φ) = 2K(x) = π·2F1(1/2,1/2;1;x^2).

(3) Fourier constant term. Write 1/√(1-x^2cos^2φ) = P + 2Q cos2φ + 2R cos4φ + 2S cos6φ + ... . Its antiderivative is Pφ + Q sin2φ + (1/2)R sin4φ + (1/3)S sin6φ + ... + C. Over [0,π] all sine terms vanish, leaving Pπ. Hence y = P: the constant term is the mean value of the function.

(4) AGM step. Since 1/y = M(1+x,1-x), one AGM step gives arithmetic mean 1 and geometric mean √(1-x^2). So 1/y = M(1,√(1-x^2)).

(5) General theorem. Let W = α/√(β - γcos^2φ) with γ > 0. Its constant term is P = (α/√β)·y(x) with x^2 = γ/β (this reduction is mine). Using homogeneity M(λa,λb) = λM(a,b):
1/P = (√β/α)·M(1,√(1-γ/β)) = M(√β/α, √(β-γ)/α).
The extreme values of W are v = α/√(β-γ) (maximum, at cos^2φ = 1) and v' = α/√β (minimum). Therefore 1/P = M(1/v, 1/v').

(6) Case γ < 0. Put ψ = 90° - φ. Then β - γcos^2φ = (β-γ) + γcos^2ψ = (β-γ) - (-γ)cos^2ψ, with -γ > 0. Part (5) then gives 1/P = M(√(β-γ)/α, √β/α), which is again M(1/max, 1/min). Shifting the integration interval is harmless because the integrand has period π.

(7) Extension to W = α/√(β + γcosφ), finished on the next page. Use cosφ = 2cos^2ψ - 1 with φ = 2ψ. Then β + γcosφ = (β-γ) + 2γcos^2ψ. The mean of W over φ in [0,2π] equals the mean over ψ in [0,π], so case (5)/(6) applies:
1/(constant term) = M(1/max W, 1/min W) = M(√(β-γ)/α, √(β+γ)/α).
The next page notes the consequence: expressions of this type with equal extreme values have equal constant terms. It also mentions the use for planetary perturbation theory, i.e. the Laplace coefficient b_{1/2}^{(0)}.
errors: Term-by-term integration of the series and the existence of the cosine expansion are assumed without justification, as was normal at the time. Both are valid for |x| < 1, or for 0 < γ < β in the general case.
The theorem tacitly requires β > γ and β > 0 (and β > |γ| in the cos φ case), so that the radicand stays positive.
Minor imprecision: 'valores maximus et minimus' presumes α > 0.
